title: Branching and boundary tests
goals: Trace the selected branch in an if elif else chain
Use indentation to identify which statements belong to a branch
Test values at and around a decision boundary
vocabulary: A possible path through a program
An expression used to decide which path to take
Leading spaces that identify a Python code block
A value where a classification may change
A previous test rerun after an edit to detect a new failure

blocks.text: These tests exercise every branch and the equality case. A change from <= 12 to < 12 is exposed by 12; testing 11 alone misses it. Branch coverage means every branch was exercised, but it does not prove every condition is correct.

blocks.label: Suppose the program uses < 12 instead of <= 12. What is printed for 12, why does that violate the written rule, and which earlier test should still pass after repair?

guided_practice.title: Trace the tested path
guided_practice.prompt: For -1, 12 and 13, record checked conditions, skipped conditions and the final label. Run each as a fresh script after predicting.
guided_practice.answer: -1: first True, second skipped, Invalid. 12: first False, second True, Short. 13: both False, else selected, Long. Retain observed results separately.

independent_case.title: Trace branch order
independent_case.task: Predict the action for 30, then trace 29 and -1. Explain why validity is checked before the lamp decision.
independent_case.answer: 30 gives off, 29 gives on, -1 gives invalid. Checking validity first prevents an invalid negative reading from being accepted as a lamp-on decision.

misconceptions: Every condition in the chain always runs
Once one condition succeeds, later alternatives are skipped.
Two if statements behave like if then elif
Independent if statements can both run and overwrite a result.
Leading spaces define the branch body.
Every branch tested means every input correct
A missing equality case can hide a wrong comparison.
